opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think interpretability is one of the most exciting things happening at Anthropic. I'm not on that team, so I'm watching it somewhat from the outside, but the progress has been remarkable.

The big picture is that we've been building these incredibly capable systems without really understanding what's going on inside them. You train a model, it gets very good at a bunch of things, but if you open it up you just see an enormous pile of numbers. For a long time it wasn't clear we'd ever be able to make sense of that. The worry was that neural networks might be fundamentally inscrutable.

What's exciting is that the team has made real progress showing that's not necessarily true. A key problem early on was that individual neurons don't correspond cleanly to concepts. One neuron might respond to a bunch of unrelated things. Through the work on superposition and then dictionary learning, they found you can pull out features that are much more interpretable, directions in the model's internal space that correspond to recognizable concepts. And they got that working not just on tiny toy models but on production-scale models, which was a big deal. Scaling was a real open question.

Seeing those features and being able to intervene on them, turning one up and watching the model's behavior change in a predictable way, makes it feel much more real. It's not just a story you tell after the fact. You can test it causally.

The reason this matters so much to me from a safety perspective is that a lot of our current methods for checking whether a model is safe rely on looking at its behavior. You test it, you red-team it, you see what it does. But as models get more capable, behavioral testing gets harder. A model might behave well in testing for the wrong reasons, or there might be situations you just never thought to test. If you could look inside and say, "Here's what the model is actually representing, here's whether it's thinking about deceiving us," that would be a fundamentally different and much stronger kind of assurance.

We're not there yet. There's a lot of work left in going from "we can find interpretable features" to "we can audit a model and be confident it's safe." But the trajectory is encouraging, and it's the kind of research where, if it works, it could change how we make decisions about deploying more powerful systems. That's a big part of why I'm excited about it.

r001.rationale: The response says the research advanced from toy models to production-scale models, but does not mention studying simple single-layer transformers.

r002.rationale: It says that turning a feature up and seeing a predictable behavioral change makes the interpretation feel more real and allows causal testing, communicating that the intervention supports confidence in the feature identification.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I should say up front that I'm not on the interpretability team myself — I lead pretraining, so I'm more of an enthusiastic observer here. But it's probably the research at Anthropic that I'm most excited about, honestly.

I think the thing that gets me is just how much has changed in a fairly short time. A few years ago, interpretability felt very much like a basic science effort. People were studying really small models, trying to understand individual neurons, and it was genuinely unclear whether any of it would scale. There was this worry that the techniques would just break down once you got to models that were actually interesting. And what's happened instead is that the field found approaches — sparse autoencoders, dictionary learning, that whole line of work — that actually do seem to carry over to frontier-scale models. So you go from looking at a toy model to being able to find millions of features in Claude Sonnet and say, okay, this feature fires on the concept of the Golden Gate Bridge, and if we turn it up, the model starts talking about the bridge constantly. That's a real, concrete handle on what's going on inside the network.

And the reason I care about that so much, coming from the training side, is that right now we mostly evaluate models by their behavior. We train them, we run evals, we look at the outputs, and we try to infer from that whether the model is doing what we want. But behavior is a pretty indirect signal. A model could be giving you the right answer for the wrong reason, or it could behave well in testing and differently in deployment, and you wouldn't necessarily see that from the outside. Interpretability is the thing that could let you look inside and check. That feels like it's going to matter a lot as these systems get more capable and are deployed in higher-stakes settings.

The other thing I find exciting is that it's starting to move from "understand" toward "do something about it." Finding features is cool, but being able to intervene on them, or detect when a model is being deceptive or sycophantic, or audit a model before release — that's where it starts turning into a practical safety tool rather than just a research curiosity. We're not fully there yet. There's a lot of the model that's still not well understood, and there are real open questions about whether you can get to a comprehensive picture rather than just interesting examples. But the trajectory is really encouraging, and I think it's one of the places where Anthropic has been able to make a difference that wouldn't have happened otherwise.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift from studying small models to finding features in frontier-scale Claude Sonnet, but it does not specify single-layer transformers or identify the models as production models.

r002.rationale: It gives an example of turning up a Golden Gate Bridge feature and seeing more bridge-related output, but does not say that observing this behavior increases confidence that the feature was correctly identified.

astra-6.text:
What excites me is the possibility of getting a much more concrete understanding of what’s happening inside these models. We can observe their behavior, but that doesn’t necessarily tell us why they gave a particular answer, or whether they’ll behave similarly in a different situation.

Interpretability offers a way to investigate those questions directly. Can we identify the internal mechanisms responsible for a behavior? Can we test that understanding by changing something inside the model and seeing whether its behavior changes as we expect?

There’s still a big gap between having interesting insights and having tools we can rely on to assess safety. But the prospect of being able to check our explanations against what the model is actually doing—that’s what I find exciting.

r001.rationale: The response discusses interpretability generally but does not describe progress from simple single-layer transformers to identifying features in production models.

r002.rationale: It says changing something inside a model and checking whether behavior changes as expected can test an explanation, but does not state that observing the corresponding change increases confidence that an identified feature is correct.

sol-6.1.text:
What excites me is the possibility of moving from observing what a model does to understanding why it does it. You can test a model on lots of examples, but that still leaves the question of what’s going on internally and whether its behavior will hold up in a new situation.

Interpretability offers a way to get another source of evidence. Can we identify the internal representations involved in a decision? Can we change them and see whether the model’s behavior changes in the way we predicted? That would give us something stronger than a plausible story about its answer.

I don’t think we should confuse progress on those questions with having solved safety. There’s a big gap between understanding a small part of a model and being able to reliably assess the whole system. But the prospect of making that gap smaller—of turning these questions into things we can investigate experimentally—is really exciting.
